newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Governor says he regrets not reassuring China.
newsitem.headline: HK Governor says he regrets not reassuring China.

text.p: British Governor Chris Patten made a farewell appearance before the territory's Legislative Council on Thursday and said he regretted not having persuaded Beijing to accept his democratic reforms.
In one of the final gasps of empire, Patten met the colony's lawmakers before China takes control of the city at midnight on June 30 and moves to scrap his controversial measures.
The last governor in a colonial interlude of more than 150 years, used rapier wit, economic statistics and diplomacy to field questions from legislators.

Asked about the biggest regret of his five-year administration Patten said he wished he had been better able to reassure Chinese leaders that the territory and its people would pose no problems for Beijing after the handover.
"Perhaps what I would like to have done was under the circumstances impossible: to convince the leaders in Beijing that there was nothing to worry about in Hong Kong," Patten told the legislators.

"(I would like to have convinced them) that the development of democratic institutions in Hong Kong...wasn't a question of planting British time bombs around the community but that it was a matter of reflecting the aspirations of the community."

Patten helped introduce democratic institutions to Hong Kong which were in sharp contrast to colonial rule during the rest of Britain's tenure here. China's communist leaders, fearing a diminution of their control after the handover, have objected to the reforms.

Chief among those new institutions was a democratically-elected Legislative Council. China is replacing that body after the handover with a Provisional Legislature chosen by a 400-member Hong Kong advisory council whose members were themselves hand-picked by Beijing.
The setting for the Governor's last legislative question period, the Legislative Council building in Statue Square, aptly symbolises the radical transformation of Hong Kong under British rule.

Built originally as a Supreme Court building, the white stone colonial structure boasts a dome and colonnades which evoke images of Hong Kong as the tranquil, sleepy outpost of empire it was for most of its history.
But the building is now dwarfed by signature office towers which embody Hong Kong's soaring economic success as a manufacturing and financial services centre for Asia and the world.
Patten was appointed Governor by then British prime minister and Conservative Party leader John Major in 1992 after he had helped engineer Major's election victory.
Several questions on Thursday dealt with the Conservative Party's massive defeat in recent British elections and Patten's political past and future. The governor used deft humour to deflect them.

Asked what he would have done had he been British prime minister over the past five years, Patten replied, to great laughter: "I think as things have turned out I would have appointed myself Governor of Hong Kong."
Confronted by a tough question challenging his stewardship over the past half-decade, Patten cited the rise of Hong Kong's Hang-Seng (stock market index) from about 5,500 to 14,200 over the period.
He also congratulated himself and his government on having introduced five successive budgets which included tax cuts, spending cuts and increases in financial reserves.
"This is a record which, if I ever go back into British politics, I hope I can repeat, which I very much doubt," Patten said.
The governor departed the council to a standing ovation from most members who rapped their desks vigorously in farewell and approval.
